analysis.one_liner: Makes federal civil asset forfeiture harder and stops agencies from keeping seized property proceeds.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan civil asset forfeiture bill, introduced with both Democratic and Republican cosponsors in February 2026, has sat in four House committees with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for civil asset forfeiture, the process by which the government takes a person's cash, car, or home suspected of being tied to a crime, even when the owner is never charged. It would require the government to tell owners within 7 days instead of 60, provide a lawyer to owners who cannot afford one, prove its case with clear and convincing evidence instead of a mere preponderance, and move every forfeiture through a federal court instead of agency paperwork. It would also end the practice of law enforcement agencies keeping the proceeds, sending them to the Treasury instead.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose property gets seized, most often cash, under suspicion of a connection to crime. Many of them are never charged with anything. They would get notice within a week, a court-appointed lawyer if they cannot afford one, a government that must meet a much higher burden of proof, a right to a prompt hearing when cash is seized over reporting rules, and a rule that no forfeiture can happen outside a federal courtroom.

how_it_helps.text: Government must notify owners of a seizure within 7 days rather than 60, and owners must be told they can contest it.
Owners who are financially unable to afford a lawyer, or for whom a lawyer would cost more than the property is worth, get appointed counsel.

The government must prove the connection between property and crime by clear and convincing evidence, a much higher bar than the current preponderance standard, and must show the owner used or knowingly allowed the property's criminal use.
No federal agency could carry out nonjudicial forfeitures; every forfeiture order would have to come from a United States district court.

Seizures tied to structuring cash transactions, a common way depositors lose money without being charged, require a probable cause hearing within 14 days of notice, with the property returned otherwise.

Equitable sharing, the channel through which federal forfeiture money flows back to state and local police, is eliminated, and proceeds go to the Treasury general fund instead of the Justice Department's own fund.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies, especially the Justice Department, lose the Assets Forfeiture Fund as a self-financing stream, and state and local police lose equitable sharing payments. Agencies contend forfeiture is a tool for dismantling drug trafficking networks and that the proceeds fund victim restitution and local enforcement. Taxpayers would also bear the cost of appointed counsel for indigent owners and of hearings the bill requires.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and local law enforcement agencies

drawbacks.text: Law enforcement argues forfeiture is a key tool against drug organizations and that redirecting proceeds away from enforcement budgets, victim restitution, and local police sharing weakens anti-crime work.
The higher evidentiary standard and mandatory counsel would make some forfeitures of genuinely criminal proceeds harder and slower, and would add costs to federal courts and taxpayers.
The bill applies retroactively to forfeiture proceedings already pending, which could unwind cases agencies have already built.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For someone who has never been charged with a crime, having cash or a car taken and having to fight a federal agency alone to get it back is a serious harm, and the current rules make that fight structurally unfair: low proof standards, long notice deadlines, and agencies that keep what they seize. The costs of this bill fall mainly on the enforcement agencies themselves and on the pace of some forfeitures. The main fair criticism is design, not principle: funding victim restitution and local drug enforcement out of forfeiture money has real value, and the bill replaces it with nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced and has not received a hearing, markup, or vote; it is still alive but has gone nowhere so far.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Walberg introduced the bill on February 20, 2026, joined from the start by Representatives Jamie Raskin, Tom McClintock, and Mary Gay Scanlon, pairing two Republicans with two Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services Committees the same day it was introduced.
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote after the referral.
Versions of the FAIR Act have been introduced in prior Congresses by the same lead sponsors and have similarly never reached a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off so far: they keep the current seizure rules, the Assets Forfeiture Fund, and equitable sharing, and property owners gain nothing until the bill moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies keep current seizure powers

against.name: House Judiciary Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has not scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: Law enforcement associations
against.what_they_did: Have opposed civil asset forfeiture reform, particularly elimination of equitable sharing, in prior debates over similar FAIR Act versions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two Republicans and two Democrats together, and its cosponsor list is mixed; with no votes yet recorded, opposition lines are not visible in the record.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (especially the DOJ)
industries.note: The bill takes away their Assets Forfeiture Fund and bans nonjudicial forfeiture, ending a system where agencies keep the proceeds of property they seize. That money currently comes largely out of the pockets of people, many never charged with a crime.

industries.industry: State, local, and tribal police departments
industries.note: Equitable sharing, the pipeline that pays local police a share of federal forfeitures, would be eliminated. These agencies have relied on that revenue, which is raised by taking property from ordinary people.
Every forfeiture moves through federal district court and indigent owners get appointed counsel, adding workload and cost to the courts but giving owners a real day in court.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to four committees with no scheduled markup rarely advance, and earlier versions of the FAIR Act in previous Congresses never reached a floor vote. Unless the Judiciary chair schedules action, this bill is likely to expire at the end of the session in January 2027 without a vote.
